question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old man with a decade-long history of cirrhosis that evolved despite regular phlebotomy for hereditary hemochromatosis was escorted to the university liver clinic by his spouse because over the past week he had taken a few extra seconds to recall the route to the grocery store, paused mid-sentence when reading the sports page aloud, and once misplaced the television remote in the refrigerator; he continued to recognize family members, dress himself, and handle basic chores but admitted to intermittent difficulty calculating the restaurant tip and to occasionally dropping coins when counting change, events that prompted today’s unscheduled visit. He denied abdominal bloating, upward pressure when bending to tie shoes, early satiety, orthopnea, pedal swelling, dark or pale stools, hematemesis, melena, bright red blood per rectum, pruritus, fevers, rash, or weight change in either direction. His past medical record included type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, mild obstructive sleep apnea treated with nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure, and remote right inguinal hernia repair; he had never experienced gastrointestinal bleeding, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, or hepatocellular carcinoma, and his only prior hospitalizations were day-procedure phlebotomies. He last drank alcohol more than fifteen years ago, has never injected drugs, quit a 20-pack-year smoking habit at age 50, and takes no herbal supplements. Medications at presentation were metformin, low-dose aspirin for primary cardiovascular prevention, a multivitamin, and occasional acetaminophen under two grams per day; he was not receiving lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, non-selective beta-blockers, albumin infusions, vitamin K, antibiotics, or proton-pump inhibitors. Allergies were limited to penicillin, which caused a rash in childhood. His father died of myocardial infarction at 71, his mother is alive with osteoporosis, and there is no family history of other liver diseases. He remains retired from a career as a postal worker, walks one mile every morning, and follows a 2-gram sodium diet advised by his dietitian. On arrival—before any venipuncture, intravenous line, or medication administration—vital signs recorded temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. He was awake, conversational, and oriented to person and place but guessed the date two days off and required prompting to recite the months backward; a low-amplitude flapping movement of the hands emerged after eight seconds when he extended his arms and dorsiflexed his wrists. Speech was fluent with normal naming, and there were no focal neurologic deficits. Breath carried a faint musty sweetness. Sclerae showed a subtle golden hue without overt icterus; one spider telangiectasia was observed over the right shoulder, and mild palmar erythema was present. The neck was supple with jugular venous pulsation 6 cm H₂O at 30°. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdominal wall was flat with preserved concavity of the umbilicus, moved symmetrically with respiration, and displayed no distention of superficial veins. Percussion produced resonant tympany throughout the central abdomen and did not shift toward dullness when the patient rolled to either side; no fluid impulse could be transmitted across the midline even without counter-pressure. The liver edge felt firm and finely nodular, palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration and non-tender; the spleen tip was not appreciated. There was no ankle or pretibial edema. Extremity muscle bulk was preserved. Digital rectal examination returned brown stool negative for occult blood. Point-of-care capillary glucose read 108 mg/dL. Following the physical examination, but still before any therapeutic intervention, bedside ultrasonography demonstrated a shrunken heterogeneous liver with capsular irregularity, patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow measuring 15 cm/s, a spleen length of 15 cm, and no echo-free fluid in the right upper quadrant, paracolic gutters, pelvis, or Morrison’s pouch; kidneys appeared normal and there was no biliary dilatation. Venous blood drawn immediately afterward revealed total bilirubin 2.35 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.42 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 46 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 72 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 182 U/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.2 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 128 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.51. Alpha-fetoprotein measured 7 ng/mL, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody remained negative, and fasting ferritin was 342 ng/mL (stable). An upright chest radiograph obtained prior to any medications showed clear lung fields without pleural effusion and a mildly elevated right hemidiaphragm, while a 12-lead electrocardiogram documented normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min with a QTc of 432 ms. No lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, albumin, vitamin K, benzodiazepines, or intravenous fluids had been provided at the time these findings were documented, thereby capturing his untreated physiologic state for ongoing assessment by the hepatology team.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points each for bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Using pretreatment findings:
- Total bilirubin 2.35 mg/dL falls in the 2–3 mg/dL range: 2 points.
- Albumin 3.42 g/dL falls in the 2.8–3.5 g/dL range: 2 points.
- INR 1.51 is below 1.7: 1 point.
- Ascites is absent on examination and ultrasound: 1 point.
- Impaired attention, slight temporal disorientation, and asterixis indicate grade I–II encephalopathy: 2 points.
Total = 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 8
